rationale: The psalm calls the Lord the portion of the speaker's inheritance and cup, and addresses Him as the One who restores the inheritance. In Numbers the Lord explicitly tells Aaron that He is Aaron's portion and inheritance; the shared portion language does not assign Aaron's land restriction to the psalmist.

relationship: Quotation that the Holy One will not see decay
rationale: Paul quotes the holy-one and decay clause and immediately distinguishes David, who saw decay, from the One God raised, who did not. This target explicitly states the resurrection application of the quoted words.

relationship: Prayer heard in relation to integrity
rationale: The speaker asks God to hear a prayer that does not come from deceitful lips. Psalm 65 joins a conditional appeal that the Lord not hear if injustice was regarded in the heart with the statement that God did hear the petition; both relate prayer and integrity.

The psalm asks to be guarded and says that God will shelter the speaker under His wings. Boaz blesses Ruth as one who has come to trust under the Lord's wings; the repeated shelter image is applied to distinct persons.

relationship: A concealed lion as the image of an attacker
rationale: The source places a lion ready for the hunt and a young lion in hiding places in its description of hostile action. Psalm 9 explicitly compares a lurking attacker with a lion in its enclosure seeking to seize a poor man; the connection concerns the concealed hunting-lion image.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines combine cherubim, flight and the wind's wings. The psalm says God flew on those wings, while Samuel says He appeared upon them after stating that He sat on cherubim and flew.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines say that the speaker will pass over a wall by his God. The first clauses differ: the psalm anticipates rescue from a raiding band, while Samuel says the speaker will run lightly armed.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines recount God giving the protection or defence of salvation. The psalm adds past right-hand support and discipline that set the speaker upright, followed by future teaching; Samuel instead names God's heeding that made him great.

relationship: Quotation of praise among the nations
rationale: Paul explicitly quotes giving thanks among the nations and singing praise to God's name while explaining Gentiles' glorifying God for mercy. The source line also has a parallel in 2 Samuel 22:50; this comparison does not decide between the two song forms as the quotation's immediate source.

relationship: Whole burnt offering and a plea for deliverance
rationale: The blessing asks God to remember every sacrifice and make the whole burnt offering fat. At Mizpah Samuel offers a whole burnt offering and cries for Israel, and the Lord hears him as the enemy approaches; this compares sacrifice joined with a plea for aid in distinct settings.

relationship: Chariots and horses contrasted with the Lord
rationale: The psalm says some rely on chariots or horses, while its speakers will be magnified in the Lord's name. Isaiah condemns reliance on Egypt's horses and chariots while failing to trust Israel's Holy One; the texts contrast military resources with God using different positive responses.

The source pictures enemies made like a fiery furnace and devoured by fire in the Lord's anger. Malachi depicts the coming day burning like an oven and the lawless as ignited straw; both use furnace or oven images for judgment while assigning the comparison to different subjects.
